title: Complexity Analysis
description: Learn Big O notation, common complexity classes, and how to reason about the performance of algorithms and data structures.

data.text: Complexity analysis measures how an algorithm's runtime or memory usage grows as the input size increases. The most common notation is Big O, which describes an upper bound on growth. Learning to read and reason about Big O helps you compare approaches, predict bottlenecks, and communicate performance trade-offs clearly.

Big O notation focuses on the dominant term in a growth function and ignores constants. For example, 3n + 5 and 100n both simplify to O(n). The goal is to understand how performance scales rather than to measure exact clock time.

data.title: Identifying Big O from code
data.content: Estimate the complexity of three simple functions.

data.text: Space complexity measures how much additional memory an algorithm needs relative to the input size. A recursive depth-first search uses O(h) stack space, where h is the height of the recursion tree. An in-place algorithm reuses the input buffer and uses O(1) extra space.

Some operations are expensive only occasionally. Amortized analysis averages the cost over a sequence of operations. A dynamic array that doubles its capacity when full has O(1) amortized insertion even though a single resize takes O(n).

data.title: Worst case vs amortized
data.text: Always clarify whether you are discussing worst-case or amortized time. An interviewer or teammate may assume worst case unless you state otherwise.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Big O describes upper-bound growth, ignoring constants.
Common classes: constant, logarithmic, linear, linearithmic, quadratic, exponential.
Space complexity measures extra memory usage.
Amortized analysis averages expensive operations over many cheap ones.
data.takeaway: Complexity analysis lets you compare algorithms objectively and predict how they will behave at scale.
